It's the largest provider of affordable housing in the country. In fact, if NYCHA were a city unto itself, it would be the largest city of low-income black and brown Americans. Or it has been at times, I think it's candidate dependent. Look, the Latino vote is not a monolith. like Puerto Ricans and Dominicans and the Bronx are different from Cubans and Venezuelans in Florida, who are different from Mexicans in California, who are different from Mexicans in in South Texas. There was scuttled by Donald Trump. That had the support of conservative Republicans and had been negotiated by conservative Senator Jim Langford from Oklahoma, and then endorsed by the Border Patrol Union. They referred to it as the strongest border control reform that had been proposed. If I can add, the compromise took us as Democrats outside our ideological comfort zone. It was the first time in recent history that Democrats agreed to a compromise on border security without any immigration reform. Typically, we insist on the coupling of the two and we decoupled and the Republicans refused to meet us in the middle. It is well established that crime is far more prevalent among legal citizens. than among migrants, and the overwhelming majority of immigrants who come here, in search for a better life, in search for economic opportunity, simply want to do right by themselves and by their families. One of the things Donald Trump said in that rally was that, actually, the people who are coming here are people who are being dumped out of jails in various countries. And we're not talking about just South America countries. We're talking about countries from Africa. Large numbers of people are coming in from China. And if you look at these people, did you see them? They are physically fit. They're 19 to 25. Almost everyone is a male. And they look like fighting age. I think they're building an army. They're 29,000 people over the last I think they're building, they want to get us from within. I think they're building an army. There are some who think that Trump uses this rhetoric because he's laying the foundation for invoking the insurrection act to use the military to round up millions of migrants if he is reelected as president. Do you think that's what he's doing? We should never underestimate the danger that Donald Trump poses to our democracy. And there's no doubt in my mind that he is so authoritarian that he is prepared to weaponize our institutions to advance his sinister political agenda. So do I know, I will claim no insight into the psyche of Donald Trump, but I do know that he has no regard for the law and he has no regard for the norms of our democracy. This week, President Biden passed an executive order. You mentioned that challenges executive orders as they can often be overturned. But this executive order is one that protects the spouses and family members of legal citizens who are not here legally. Is this a helpful step for President Biden? It's the right thing to do. You know, whether it's wise politically as a separate question, but... Do you think it's not? But there's no clear, I don't know, but there's no clear distinction. There's not necessarily a clear distinction between legal citizens and undocumented immigrants. There are countless mixed status households in America that include people who have legal status and have no status at all. And it's in our interest to keep those families together. Like whether you're a Republican or a Democrat, we all should be pro-family. We should all should be in favor of preserving the American family, including those that have mixed status. So I support the president's executive order to the extent that it strengthens the American family. You have been described as Israel's loudest supporter in the House of Representatives. You're not Jewish. But you've been Jewish, I suppose. But you've been described as a loyal ally since you first visited Israel in 2015. How do you explain to folks who just have to think twice about a gay, Christian, Afro reporter weekend member of Congress who is so passionately Zionist? Well, first, one need not be Jewish to combat anti-Semitism, just like one need not be black to combat anti-black racism. And as you know, throughout history, there have been Jews who gave their lives for the cause of civil rights. Right 60 years ago, Michael Schwarner and Andrew Goodman, as well as James Cheney, were barbarically murdered in the Mississippi burning so that black Americans could live freely. unencumbered by the cruelty of Jim Crow. And so for me, the lesson learned from history is that we're all in this together and we all have an obligation to fight extremism and anti-Semitism, no matter what form it takes, no matter what direction from which it comes. But I will confess that I am an improbable Zionist because for all of my childhood, I grew up in a community that was exclusively African-American and Latino. I had no engagement with the Jewish community, no knowledge of Zionism or Judaism. But a turning point came in 2014 when I served in the city council. I was invited by the Jewish Community Relations Council and affiliate of UJA to go on a delegation to Israel. It was the first time I had an opportunity to travel abroad. And when I went to Israel, when I went to Yad Vashem, the Holocaust Museum, when I went to the Masada, where Jews famously committed mass suicide in order to escape enslavement at the hands of the Roman Empire, when I went to the Gaza Envelope, it was a transformative experience. And I remember speaking to the mayor of State Road in the Gaza Envelope in the south, who said that the majority of his children struggle with post-traumatic stress, because families like his live under this red or relentless rocket fire. And I remember seeing bus stops doubling as bomb shelters. And I thought to myself, imagine the sheer trauma of an Israeli child seeking refuge in a bomb shelter, or rockets are being fired while sirens are going off while adults are panicking in a state of pandemonium. I come from the Bronx where people live in fear of guns, bullets, but no one in the United States lives in fear of rockets. Like none of us worry that Mexico and Canada are gonna fire rockets into American homes and communities. And so I came to realize early on that Israel faces a level of insecurity that has no analog in the American experience. You have around your neck a pendant that says bring them home. Tell me about it. Look, for me, the greatest moral imperative is to secure the release of the hostages. You know, we live in a world of rapidly growing amnesia about October 7th. We as Americans have forgotten that there are American hostages languishing in Hamas territories under captivity. And we owe it to our fellow Americans to do everything we can to secure their release and to bring them home. And home is not only Israel, it's the United States of America. And I find it frustrating that the international community has been aggressively pressuring Israel to keep Hamas in power. But far fewer have been pressuring Hamas to release the hostages. And the international pressure has been so overwhelmingly one-sided against Israel that Hamas has felt emboldened to delay the release of the hostages and delay the end of the war. If Hamas were to release the hostages and surrender unconditionally, the war would end immediately. Like Hamas has the power to end the war it began and to release the hostages, it abducted. You recently were slightly critical of President Biden for withholding or pausing arms from Israel. And at times suggested he was pandering to the left. Are you concerned that his support for Israel is wavering? President Biden, for me, has been the most pro-Israel president in American history. He's the first president to go to Israel. He's the first president to go to Israel in a time of war. He sent out one but two carriers to the Mediterranean to deter threats like Hezbollah. And he has managed to sustain support for Israel for more than eight months. which no other president has ever had to do. And he's done so under the scrutiny of social media and 24 seven cable news. He's done so despite resistance from the far left of the party. Like, do I agree with everything the president has said or done? No, but to critique every minute decision is to miss the forest for the trees. When you examine the grand scheme of what the president has done, he is fundamentally pro-Israel and has been a friend of the Jewish state. So that those critiques are critiques, not criticisms that you. Constructive criticisms. And my concern was not so much about the withholding of the weapons. It was publicly signaling, declining support for Israel. Like we have to recognize there are two wars unfolding. There's the Warren Gaza, but there's also an information war unfolding on social media platforms. We have to be mindful of the words we speak. And if we signal to the world, that American support for Israel might show signs of wavering, then we are unwittingly playing into the hands of Hamas. So I would ask all elected officials to be mindful of the information war. It may surprise some people that you've recently split with the progressive movement. You said, I didn't leave the progressive movement. The progressive movement left me. You received some pushback for the comments. I'm shocked. And a New York Magazine column said, quote, you had chosen the powerful over the powerless. How did the progressive movement lose you? Well, first, when I entered public office back in, when I first ran back in 2013, the progressive position on policing was police reform. Today, it's become defunding the police or abolishing the police. Back then, the progressive policing on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict was the two-state solution. Now it's BDS or one-state solution to the exclusion of Israel. And so I have felt alienated from what the progressive movement has become because it has become radicalized. What people want in the Bronx is not under-policing or over-policing, but better policing, more accountable and more transparent policing. What people in the Bronx want is peace between the Israelis and Palestinians. We all want to choose Christians and Muslims to coexist in peace and prosperity, which is why I'm so passionate about the Abraham Accords. So I'm far more pragmatic. The fundamental problem with the modern progressive movement is that it has let progressive purity be the enemy of progress in the real world. Give me an example. You know, George, I'll quote, George Orwell. George Orwell once said, there are some ideas that are so stupid that only intellectuals can believe them. And, you know, the idea of abolishing the police has more currency in academia, more currency among academics and activists than working class people of color who represent the heart and soul of the Democratic Party. You said that blockchain, quote, blockchain technology can liberate the lowest income communities from the highest fees of the traditional financial system. How can blockchain empower people in your district or blockchain technologies and cryptocurrencies and these new technologies empower people from your district? So I'm a techno optimist. For me, there's been no greater catalyst for human progress, for economic growth than technology. Technology at its core is a tool for solving problems. It can be a tool for lifting up the vulnerable if we put it to constructive use. And blockchain technology is no exception. Blockchain has the potential to revolutionize the internet, creating a new layer of the internet known as Web3. And it has the potential to revolutionize finance, creating a better, cheaper, faster payment system. So I represent the Bronx, which historically has been left behind by the traditional financial system. 20% of the Bronx is unbanked, 30% is underbanked. More than a decade ago, the Department of Consumer Affairs in New York did a study and found that low-income New Yorkers spend more than $200 million a year in check-hashing fees in places like the Bronx. So I represent immigrants who pay exorbitant fees simply to transfer remittance, simply to transfer their own money to their loved ones abroad because we have a financial system that is so heavily intermediated and so full of rent-seeking And so there are two innovations that can revolutionize the financial system. One is blockchain, which enables direct real time transactions, no need for intermediaries. And stablecoin has the power to digitize the dollar, to put the dollar on the blockchain. And so I feel the ability to move a digital dollar at the real time speed of the blockchain has the potential to liberate the lowest income families from the high fees and long delays of the traditional financial system. So what would need to happen for that to become a reality? So in order for technology to thrive, you need regulatory clarity. For me, it's fundamentally unfair for, it would be unfair for the government to ticket you for speeding without telling you the speeding limit. And there are entrepreneurs in the crypto space and in the blockchain space who have no clarity about the rules that govern their industry. So Congress has a responsibility to create a framework for regulating cryptocurrencies, a framework that enables the best actors to innovate while holding the worst actors to account and filtering them out of the industry. And that's what we should do. If we had a regulatory framework that provides clarity then crypto innovation has a fighting chance of flourishing in the United States. And we are lagging behind the rest of the world when it comes to sensible crypto regulation. Who's done it best? There are a number of countries, but it's interesting. Typically, the United States out-innovates the rest of the world and Europe out-regulates the rest of the world. And it's the opposite when it comes to crypto that Europe has actually been more thoughtful about regulation and striking the balance between regulation and innovation. Does that fall under the financial services jurisdiction? Most, it's this split jurisdiction. So there are two market regulators, the CFTC which regulates commodities, the SEC which regulates securities, and there's a debate. which cryptocurrencies qualify as commodities and which qualify as securities. And so the purpose of a regulatory framework is to identify which are commodities, which are securities, and what is the process by which a crypto security can become a commodity. Those are definitions that can only be provided by an act of Congress because there's conflict between our regulators. The CFTC has said that Ether is a commodity. The SEC has said that Ether is a security. Well, those two definitions under federal law are mutually exclusive. So if you're receiving conflicting directives from the two market regulators, how can you possibly comply with federal law? And so Congress has to referee the dispute and provide a regulatory framework that clarifies which cryptocurrencies fall into which jurisdiction. Realistically, do you see that kind of clarity coming from Congress in the next two to four years? Look, we passed a regulatory framework for crypto in the house and the vote was far more bipartisan than people expected. It had the support of former speaker Nancy Pelosi, it had the support of a number of members in democratic leadership, Katherine Clark, Pedagular. So there was a growing bipartisan consensus in favor of crypto regulation that would bring clear rules of the road. You have spoken really pointedly about your own struggles with mental health. You referenced that you dropped out of college. Of course, you had been enrolled at NYU. You had been a stellar high school student. What have you learned about mental health that impacts how you think about public policy related to mental health? Well, for one thing, mental health is nothing of which to be ashamed. And I've been honest about my struggles. About 15 years ago, I found myself at the lowest point in my life. I had dropped out of college NYU, found myself struggling with depression. I even attempted suicide under wind hospitalization. I felt as if the world around me had collapsed. And as a result of receiving mental health care, I rebuilt my life. and I put myself on a new trajectory and seven years later I became the youngest elected official in America's largest city and then seven years later became a member of the United States Congress. Every day I wake up and I take an antidepressant and I feel no shame in admitting it. I'm living proof that mental healthcare can enable you to be the best version, the most productive version of yourself, even in a highly pressurized environment like the United States Congress. And so I feel like the central lesson of my story is that even in your moment of greatest despair, I never lose hope. I feel like only in America is a story like mine possible. So I feel like the most grateful person on Earth, and I've risen on the strength of mental health care. Representative Richard Torres, thank you for joining the Enfiring Line, and thank you for your service. It's an honor to be here.
